article_title: Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Five implementation challenges of delivering LLI in secondary schools
description: The Oakland evaluation enumerates five challenges schools faced implementing LLI at the secondary level: "delayed start dates and varying end dates", "tradeoffs between pullout groups and scheduled classes", "skipped and modified lesson components", "limited teacher training", and "students’ attendance and engagement at the high school level". This enumerated list characterizes how a packaged elementary-grade intervention translates imperfectly to secondary scheduling and engagement contexts.
requirements: Schools must schedule LLI sessions without displacing grade-level classes and must train teachers in the program.
constraints: Challenges were documented in Oakland secondary schools; the brief does not claim they generalize to elementary settings.
target_learners: Secondary students reading multiple years below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and English language arts/literacy standards mastery
examples: In Oakland, schools delayed starts, varied end dates, traded off pullout groups against scheduled classes, skipped or modified lesson components, provided limited teacher training, and struggled with high-school attendance and engagement.
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/leveled-literacy-intervention-for-secondary-students-results-from-a-randomized-controlled-trial

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: LLMs extend the instructional intelligence axis through semantic understanding without manual knowledge engineering
description: The chapter argues that large language models address the knowledge-engineering bottleneck that historically bounded instructional intelligence. LLMs are "AI systems trained on large collections of text to develop a broad understanding of language, concepts, and their relationships." For serious games this enables four capabilities previously requiring manual authoring: natural language interaction with unstructured learner input, context-sensitive explanation generation, grounded content generation via retrieval-augmented generation, and metacognitive scaffolding through Socratic prompts and worked-example variations.
requirements: Grounded content generation requires retrieval-augmented generation combining LLM language capabilities with access to validated domain sources such as medical protocols and assessment rubrics
constraints: LLMs provide reactive intelligence without proactive pedagogical control: they do not inherently maintain persistent learner models or pursue long-term pedagogical objectives
LLM outputs are sensitive to prompt formulation, creating reproducibility and reliability challenges
LLMs may generate confident, fluent content that is factually incorrect (hallucination risk), particularly serious in high-stakes domains
target_learners: Learners in serious games across healthcare, defense, and education domains
target_learning_goals: Semantic understanding of unstructured learner responses, context-sensitive feedback, and metacognitive scaffolding
examples: In healthcare simulation, LLMs allow virtual patients to respond naturally to open-ended history-taking questions rather than requiring multiple-choice menu selection
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education
citation: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095
title: LLM-backed Chrome extension surfacing AI feedback drafts within Gradescope
description: A lightweight, LLM-backed Chrome extension integrated into the Gradescope grading platform, powered by o4-mini (selected via Bradley-Terry analysis of TA rankings). After grading, TAs click a "Done Grading" button inserted by the extension; in treatment submissions a personalized AI feedback draft is shown, which TAs "can use the feedback draft as-is, edit it, or ignore it." The extension also logs behavioral data (provision, length, time) and embeds in-situ surveys on draft usage and helpfulness.
requirements: Integration with an existing grading platform (Gradescope)
A prompt incorporating problem description, instructor solution, grading rubric, and student submission
constraints: Drafts shown only after grading to reduce over-reliance, per instructor and formative-study input
target_learners: teaching assistants grading written assessments in higher education
target_learning_goals: increasing personalized feedback provision on student submissions
examples: A pilot during a practice assignment (HW0) validated the extension and integration plan with no issues requiring changes

title: LLM-based web agent that engages with an online learning experience like a student and generates a description of the student experience
description: The article creates a web agent built on LLMs that "engages with an online learning experience much like a student would – autonomously navigating the interface and analyzing the website content". It then "generates a comprehensive description of the student experience", which the authors use both to predict student outcomes and to give designers feedback on lesson designs. The agent is positioned as an efficient, low-cost stand-in for early-stage design feedback.

target_learners: Online learners in massive open-access CS1 courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving the student experience of online lessons
examples: The agent autonomously navigated the interface and analyzed website content of an online CS1 course lesson, producing descriptions used to predict dropout.

article_title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
citation: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas.
title: Large language models as apparatuses of power-knowledge that produce structured accounts reflecting distributions of authority in training data
description: Applying Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, the paper argues LLMs are not neutral retrieval tools but systems that are productive of knowledge and constitutive of the subjects who encounter it. The authors state: "Large language models and generative AI technologies are a new apparatus of power-knowledge within this frame." Generated responses produce a probabilistically structured account reflecting the distributions of authority and legitimacy within training data, including the dominance of peer-reviewed, English-language, Western-produced, and formally published sources.
requirements: Users must be equipped to recognize and interrogate the encoding of power in AI outputs, since the question is not whether AI systems encode power but whether users can name what a system cannot or will not represent
constraints: The authors note this is not a claim that AI systems are simply biased in the pejorative sense, but that all knowledge systems are selective and selectivity is always a form of power
target_learners: Users of generative AI systems in education, healthcare, and research
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI produces what it presents as knowledge and interrogating its structuring assumptions
examples: The paper links inability to recognize what a system cannot represent to Fricker's hermeneutical injustice, which AI systems risk reproducing and scaling
key_sources: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547

article_title: AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized
citation: Calvin Isley, Johann D. Gaebler, and Sharad Goel. (2026). AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22549
title: LLM-based pipeline converting unstructured application materials into structured measures, including a seven-dimension essay quality score validated against expert ratings
description: The authors built an LLM-based pipeline that converts unstructured application materials (transcripts, recommendation letters, resumes, essays) into structured measures, extracting 216 measures designed with admissions officers. Essay quality is scored along seven dimensions—"grammar, style, clarity, prompt responsiveness, voice, commitment to public service, and demonstrated leadership"—each graded on a five-point scale, then combined into a composite score fitted to predict expert ratings from five admissions officers. The automated and expert ratings correlate at 70%. The pipeline also produced 427 covariates used in the causal models.
requirements: Requires LLM scoring prompts with concrete rubric criteria per dimension and expert calibration ratings from admissions officers to fit dimension weights
constraints: The authors state the automated quality measure is an imperfect proxy for expert judgment and may systematically miss dimensions of quality that matter in admissions
target_learning_goals: accurate structured assessment of applicant writing quality and application materials
examples: Five admissions officers each rated up to 100 essays (50 likely human, 50 likely AI) on a six-point scale to calibrate the composite score; the resulting LLM-based rating correlated 70% with expert ratings (Fig. 2).
key_sources: Calvin Isley, Johann D. Gaebler, and Sharad Goel. (2026). AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22549

article_title: WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant
citation: Andrew Ash and John Hu. (2026). WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02420
title: LLM-assisted hardware debugging protocol mapped to the four-step troubleshooting model
description: The paper proposes a protocol following Katz and Anderson's troubleshooting model, in which an LLM-assistant supports each of the four steps: "understanding the system, testing the system, locating the bug, and ﬁxing the bug." The LLM summarizes datasheets and expected component functionality, helps draft test plans, generates multiple potential root causes, and reminds the student of hardware context while fixing and verifying the bug. The student must maintain control by validating the LLM's claims throughout.
requirements: The student must maintain control of the interaction by validating the LLM's claims to ensure it has an accurate understanding of the hardware
The student needs patience and endurance, and must commit to assertively correcting the LLM's misunderstandings
constraints: Prompting strategies will change as LLM models are regularly updated and improved
target_learners: electrical and computer engineering students debugging circuits in labs and projects
examples: In the study, the LLM provided accurate hardware information during system understanding, helped draft test plans, generated potential root causes from test results, and helped draft functionality tests after the fix
key_sources: Andrew Ash and John Hu. (2026). WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02420

article_title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
citation: Pardos ZA, Bhandari S (2024) ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills. PLoS ONE 19(5): e0304013. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0304013
title: LLM-generated tutoring content should be adopted where the LLM can answer the domain's questions with near-zero error, since autonomous generation suits domains the model scores highly in
description: The article argues that because worked solutions depend on the LLM answering correctly, "the domains for which an effective, autonomously-produced tutor could be generated will correspond to those in which the LLM can score highly on tests." With self-consistency yielding near-zero algebra error, the authors state that subject area is "primed for completely autonomous educational content generation," which could alleviate the most time- and cost-intensive component of tutoring system development.
requirements: Verification that LLM error in the target domain is near zero, e.g. via error mitigation and quality checks
constraints: The study's scope was limited to secondary and early post-secondary mathematics and to text-only problems without graphical figures
target_learners: secondary and early post-secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: algebra and statistics problem-solving with worked-solution hints
examples: ChatGPT hints were produced in 1/20th the time of human tutor-authored hints while producing statistically inseparable learning gains

title: LLM-based scientific document translation system with domain-specific terminology glossaries
description: The first CRITICS component is an LLM-based scientific document translation system intended to surpass conventional MT approaches, which often struggle with domain-specific terminology and notation. It uses "adapters fine-tuned on specialized scientific corpora to preserve structural elements and field-specific terminology". The project will develop domain-specific terminology glossaries integrated through prompt engineering or fine-tuning datasets, and tools to preserve layout, citations, equations, code and section formatting in translations.

article_title: A Taxonomy of LLM-Supported Tasks for Critical AI Literacy in Journalism
citation: Laurence Dierickx, Fredrik Bjerknes, Andreas L. Opdahl, Carl-Gustav Lindén. (2026). A Taxonomy of LLM-Supported Tasks for Critical AI Literacy in Journalism. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00690-0
title: A workflow-based taxonomy of LLM-supported journalistic tasks across four news-production stages
description: The paper introduces a conceptual taxonomy that translates journalistic work into computationally informed tasks framed by journalism ethics. The paper states it introduces "a task-based taxonomy that draws on task definitions from machine learning and natural language processing, framed by journalism ethics." Journalistic work is organised into four stages mirroring news production, and within each stage tasks are linked to baseline prompts, ethical risks, and mitigation strategies so students can use LLMs critically while maintaining editorial standards. Each task category is articulated through a model-agnostic prompt baseline situated within a risk-based ethical framework.
requirements: Task categories must correspond to recognisable journalistic activities and be refined iteratively against newsroom practice, following an abductive logic moving between theoretical concepts and practical use cases
constraints: The paper acknowledges the taxonomy is not exhaustive and requires validation in classroom settings, and should be regarded as a pedagogical resource rather than a prescriptive model
target_learners: non-expert users of LLMs in journalism education
target_learning_goals: ethical reasoning about AI-assisted news work
examples: Tables 2-5 define tasks per stage, e.g. extraction with a prompt to list and classify elements, with risks such as misclassification and mitigations such as manual review against the initial source

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: LLM-based project skill extraction workflow using a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 instruct model
description: A component that parses sponsor-provided project descriptions and asks an LLM to rate the necessity of each skill on a 0–5 scale, where "a 5 is given when a skill is realistically indispensable for a project." The implementation "uses a preexisting fine-tuned instruct version of Llama 3.2" and produces "a structured JSON list of skills and their rated necessity, that is then manually reviewed and given minor or no corrections." The prompt includes caveats about multiple possible solution paths (e.g., Pytorch or Tensorflow) so the model considers multiple potential solutions.
requirements: The same skill list given to students is sent to the LLM with each project description
Manual review of the LLM's structured JSON skill ratings
constraints: The article notes LLM-generated project skills still require manual verification
target_learning_goals: accurate skill-to-project alignment in team formation
examples: Applied to sponsor-submitted capstone project descriptions at UC Merced

title: 30-minute LLM demystification lesson introducing how LLMs work and research on their learning effects
description: A 30-minute lesson added in the second week of the CS2 course explaining that LLMs are a machine learning model, a Transformer doing next-token prediction, and that LLMs do not think or problem solve. It "highlighted the CS education research on how LLM use can affect student learning" and included a ChatGPT-generated example of risks such as shallow understanding and inhibited debugging skills. The authors state the lesson can be used in a variety of courses.
requirements: Adaptation from an existing introductory-course lesson with more detail on how LLMs work, plus CS education research references
constraints: The demystify lesson itself is broadly reusable, unlike the course-specific assessment changes
target_learners: undergraduate CS students in introductory programming and data structures courses
target_learning_goals: building an informed mental model of LLMs
avoiding over-trust of LLMs and shortcuts to learning
examples: The lesson explained next-token prediction, emphasized LLMs do not think or problem solve, and presented an example of risks for a CS2 student generated by ChatGPT

article_title: Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2
citation: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908
title: Allow LLM use with required attribution while increasing the weight of proctored assessments with retakes to guard against over-reliance
description: Rather than banning or unconditionally allowing LLMs, the course permits their use with a required attribution statement on every code file, while grade weight shifts from programming assignments to proctored assessments with retakes. The authors state this approach "allows the use of LLMs but with assessment design to provide guardrails against over-reliance," so students can still meet learning objectives without assistance. The attribution statement's final sentence makes students responsible for completing work unassisted.
requirements: In-class proctored retakes of each test, with question banks of assignment-aligned questions created over a summer with UTA support
Office-hours test review with a TA or instructor after the first attempt
constraints: Assessment alignment with programming assignments is course specific and time-intensive; generating question variations was not reliable without oversight
target_learners: instructors of large introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: independent mastery of course learning outcomes
examples: The CS2 course reallocated 20% of the grade from programming assignments (45% to 25%) to proctored assessments (35% to 55%), used two tests each with a retake day one week later, and required per-file attribution statements

article_title: Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University
citation: Dumlao, J. M. Z., Wang, M., Xie, Z., Hu, J., Bar, I., Chaney, G., III, Gold, H., & Teplitskiy, M. (2026). Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21534
title: Human-validated LLM annotation pipeline reconstructing assessment weights from syllabi to measure course GenAI susceptibility
description: The pipeline converts syllabus PDFs to Markdown and uses an LLM through a university-managed API gateway to reconstruct final-grade weights for each assessment category, which feed the continuous GenAI-susceptibility treatment variable. The authors use "reconstruction" rather than extraction because LLMs "generate labels that are likely to match the document". Validation against a stratified human-annotated sample found strong recovery, with susceptibility reconstructed at a mean absolute error of 0.063 on the 0–1 scale.
requirements: Requires syllabus PDFs and a university-managed API gateway approved for moderately sensitive data; validation relies on two trained human coders per syllabus with consensus resolution
constraints: Unknown exams are assumed non-susceptible by default; projects with unspecified presentation weightings are split equally between susceptible and non-susceptible
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students at a large U.S. public university
target_learning_goals: measuring course assessment structures to study effects of GenAI availability on grades and satisfaction
examples: Applied to 36,357 syllabi from 2015–2025 to compute the proportion of each course offering's final grade determined by GenAI-susceptible assignments

article_title: Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use
citation: Liu, A., Sun, M., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., & He, K. (2026). Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use. https://osf.io/ju59q/overview?view_only=96afb71945044b8794e113f9763cc74a
title: Division of interpretive labor: the LLM as a labeling instrument, not an interpretive agent, with humans retaining conceptual authority
description: The article's organizing methodological framework positions the LLM as a component whose contributions are inspected rather than trusted: it generates candidate labels, structured annotations, and suggested unifications, while researchers decide what enters, merges, or is discarded in the codebook. As the authors put it, "the model's role was confined to proposing, and the researchers' role was to dispose." This human-in-the-loop stance is presented as the safeguard that keeps the interpretive chain of custody intact, absorbs model changes between phases, and makes sites of potential model bias inspectable.
requirements: Human researchers must read raw data alongside model outputs, memo decisions including misleading model proposals, and confront the instrument with data no model preprocessed
constraints: Model-proposed candidate labels are not strictly reproducible across commercial model versions; designs in which model output is itself the finding lack this protection
target_learners: Qualitative researchers considering LLM assistance in codebook development
target_learning_goals: Preserving human interpretive authority while scaling qualitative coding of large interaction corpora
examples: The pipeline crossed a model change from Claude 3 Sonnet to Claude 3.5 Haiku between the axial and selective phases without threatening validity because outputs were always subject to human disposition.

article_title: Large language models as grading assistants in public health education: a method-comparison study of essay-style exam assessment
citation: Brevik A, Jerpseth H and Lafontan SR (2026). Large language models as grading assistants in public health education: a method-comparison study of essay-style exam assessment. Front. Educ. 11:1904452. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904452
title: Use LLMs as supervised grading assistants rather than autonomous graders for essay-style exams
description: The article concludes that LLMs can support essay grading in health sciences education but only under human oversight. It reports that "LLMs may currently be better suited as supervised grading assistants than as autonomous graders," because moderate agreement with humans combined with session-to-session variability makes default-setting autonomous grading unreliable for high-stakes assessment. The principle directs implementation toward assistance, verification, and efficiency support rather than replacement of human judgment.
requirements: Human oversight and transparency when integrating LLMs into educational assessment
Verification of LLM-suggested grades by human examiners before grades are finalized
constraints: Autonomous LLM-based grading using default settings is not currently reliable for high-stakes assessment tasks
Agreement was sensitive to operational conditions including prompt context, file upload volume, and repeated execution
target_learners: master's-level public health and health sciences students
target_learning_goals: reliable grading of long-form, essay-style exam answers
examples: The study compared LLM-assigned A-F grades with published human grades on 32 anonymized master's exam submissions and found only moderate, unstable alignment.
key_sources: Brevik A, Jerpseth H and Lafontan SR (2026). Large language models as grading assistants in public health education: a method-comparison study of essay-style exam assessment. Front. Educ. 11:1904452. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904452

article_title: What Students Ask Matters: LLM Interaction Depth, Task Quality, and Immediate Recall in Higher Education
citation: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6
title: Privacy-preserving instrumentation pipeline linking LLM conversational telemetry to learning outcomes
description: A replicable, GDPR-aligned pipeline that records every prompt and response in a custom Streamlit application backed by Gemini 1.5 Flash, generating a random six-character pseudonymous ID that links logs, assessments, and submissions without personally identifiable information. The article states it "demonstrates a replicable, privacy-preserving instrumentation pipeline that links anonymised conversational telemetry with assessment data under GDPR-aligned conditions". Logs carry millisecond timestamps, character counts, and latency metrics, written to an append-only Google Sheet and exported as CSV for scripted preprocessing with validity checks.

title: LLM Reliance Scale: 20-item, four-subscale instrument distinguishing reliance type from reliance intensity

citation: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109
title: Multi-agent LLM qualitative coding pipeline and open-source discussion dataset
description: The authors developed and released a baseline pipeline in which "AI agents simulate the collaborative coding process of human coders": an excerpt-extraction preprocessing step, independent coding by two LLM coders with justified decisions and present/absent/undecidable options, up to three rounds of debate on conflicting cases, derivation of new labeling rules, and a final re-coding pass with Cohen's Kappa computed each round. They used OpenAI's ChatGPT with the 'gpt-4o-mini' model, temperature 0 for coding and 0.7 for discussions, across four datasets (education, law, sociology, medicine) with five labels and 500 instances per label. The prompt design, pipeline, and LLM-generated discussions are released as open-source materials.

article_title: The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows
citation: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807
title: The LLM fallacy: a cognitive attribution error in which LLM-assisted outputs are misattributed as evidence of independent competence
description: The article introduces the LLM fallacy as "a cognitive attribution error in which individuals misinterpret LLM-assisted outputs as evidence of their own independent competence, producing a systematic divergence between perceived and actual capability." It distinguishes the construct from hallucination, automation bias, and cognitive offloading: unlike those, it concerns how outputs are absorbed into self-assessment rather than output correctness or reliance. The paper positions it as an extension of self-assessment error research to hybrid human-AI workflows.
requirements: The task must involve LLM-mediated output generation producing content that would otherwise require domain expertise
The interaction must be seamless enough that the human-input/system-output distinction is not salient
The output must exhibit fluency or coherence typically associated with skilled human performance
constraints: A conceptual construct; the article states empirical validation is still needed

target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive self-assessment of one's own competence when using AI assistance

citation: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807
title: Mechanistic framework: opacity, fluency, and immediacy produce capability divergence via attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing
description: The article proposes a mechanism in which LLM interaction properties — opacity (hidden generation process), fluency (surface-level coherence), and interactional immediacy — shape cognitive mediation processes of attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing, which produce misattribution and capability divergence. As Figure 1 summarizes, capability divergence (ΔC) "emerges from the interaction of system-level properties, namely opacity, fluency, and immediacy, mediated by attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing." Pipeline opacity prevents users from tracing how outputs are produced, while fluency acts as a heuristic metacognitive cue.
requirements: Repeated LLM-mediated workflows in which intermediate generative steps are not visible to the user
constraints: Proposed conceptual account; the article frames it as motivating systematic empirical investigation
target_learners: Users of LLM systems in knowledge work
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI interaction shapes metacognitive monitoring and self-attribution

description: The article introduces a multi-domain typology in which the same attributional mechanism takes different forms: in the computational domain, execution is misread as technical competence; in the linguistic domain, users conflate fluency with internalized language ability; in the epistemic domain, access to summaries is equated with mastery, "aligns with the illusion of explanatory depth"; and in professional signaling, users report LLM-assisted outputs as independent skill. citation: Sebastian Maier, Kai Schwabe, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel. (2026). Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20143
title: Custom LLM practice platform with validated offloading classifier for extent-of-support labeling
description: The article built a custom web platform (React frontend, Python backend, PostgreSQL) giving full experimental control and logging of a fraction-arithmetic learning session with an LLM assistant built on GPT-OSS-120B accessed via Amazon Bedrock at temperature 0. A custom LLM-based offloading classifier, combined with a rule-based numerical check, labeled the highest level of support requested per item across four levels: no AI use, guided help, intermediate result, and complete answer. title: Integrated LLM-plus-consortium-blockchain architecture for accountable online education
description: The article proposes a framework in which "LLM based services provide the intelligent educational interface, while a permissioned consortium blockchain serves as a secure and tamper proof ledger". The LLM layer delivers conversational tutoring, content generation, and automated grading; the blockchain layer records enrollments, grades, certificates, and AI-mediated actions as tamper-evident transactions governed by smart contracts, so AI errors are immutably logged and traceable for accountability. The integration is bidirectional: the AI personalizes instruction using the learner's verifiable on-chain history, while every AI output is anchored on-chain.
requirements: A consortium of authorized institutions (e.g., universities and education authorities) must collectively operate the blockchain nodes and share governance
constraints: Low-risk tutoring interactions are not recorded on-chain to protect privacy; recording learner consultation logs is optional and configurable
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
examples: The prototype couples a lightweight LMS front-end with an automated tutoring and grading engine, committing every critical event to a Hyperledger Fabric consortium ledger with off-chain feedback anchored by cryptographic hashes

article_title: Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing
citation: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303
title: LLM-compiled wiki knowledge representation over an authentic course corpus
description: An ingest-time knowledge representation in which a course corpus is compiled into a linked wiki: "concept pages synthesized by an LLM, cross links between related pages, and citations from every page back to the raw sourcematerials." At query time the LLM navigates and reads relevant pages rather than receiving similarity-ranked chunks. In this study it covered 12 pages (7 course concept pages such as K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, and ML Bias & Fairness, plus 5 navigational/meta pages) built from a frozen DS3001/DS3021 corpus snapshot, and served as Arm B in the head-to-head comparison against vector RAG.
requirements: The corpus must be compiled at ingest into linked concept pages with explicit cross references and citations back to raw source materials, with the context budget matched across comparison arms.
constraints: Generalization is untested beyond a single course corpus (DS3001) and its topic mix; the evaluated wiki covered only the subset of DS 3021 compiled into 12 pages.
target_learning_goals: answering course questions grounded in vetted course materials
tracing claims back to source lectures and readings
examples: Arm B compiled the same DS3001/DS3021 corpus used by the vector RAG control into a raw/+wiki/ structure, and the LLM navigated wiki pages at query time while Arm A retrieved top-k chunks from a 21-vector index.

article_title: Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions
citation: Grion, Valentina; Doria, Beatrice; Agostini, Daniele; Slaviero, Giorgia. (2026). Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions. Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education. https://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2697962
title: AI-generated feedback from GPT-o4-mini and DeepSeek R1 as formative assessment components in a project-based university course
description: This element is feedback generated by two large language models, GPT-o4-mini and DeepSeek R1, delivered in place of or alongside expert teacher feedback in a project-based university course. The study examined "the effectiveness and practical comparability of AI-generated feedback," assigning 47 student groups (N = 238) to one of three feedback conditions and analysing changes with non-parametric tests, robust models, and non-inferiority and equivalence analyses. Student perceptions were additionally collected from 200 students via a validated questionnaire.
requirements: a project-based course with explicit criteria enabling comparable feedback generation
expert teacher feedback as the comparison benchmark
constraints: performance was measured at project level for groups, not individuals
examples: students received AI or teacher feedback on project work, with pre- to post-feedback performance compared across conditions

citation: Mireia Vendrell, Samantha-Kaye Johnston. (2026). Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100572
title: A design-oriented pedagogical framework for integrating LLMs to scaffold critical thinking in higher education
description: The article proposes a normative, design-oriented framework grounded in Design-Based Research, instructional-design theory, AI ethics and Freirean critical pedagogy. It links three risks of unstructured LLM use to six intellectual processes and eight design principles, arguing that 'the value of generative AI in education is not technical but fundamentally pedagogical'. It positions LLMs as objects of inquiry learners must interrogate rather than as tutors or efficiency supports.
requirements: Requires deliberate instructional sequencing and alignment of principles with the cognitive, metacognitive and epistemic processes they support
constraints: The authors state the framework 'is not intended as a definitive or universal solution, but as provisional pedagogical orientation that must remain open to critique, adaptation, and contextual interpretation'
examples: Two illustrative classroom scenarios (prompt design and AI-mediated argument construction) operationalise the framework's principles

article_title: LLMs Do Not Grade Essays Like Humans
citation: Jerin George Mathew, Sumayya Taher, Anindita Kundu, Denilson Barbosa. (2026). LLMs Do Not Grade Essays Like Humans. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23714
title: Framework combining LLM scoring, generated feedback, and essay-feature analysis
description: The article proposes an analysis framework in which "Essays are first evaluated by LLMs to produce both predicted scores and textual feedback." Essay-level features (length, Flesch Reading Ease readability, and LanguageTool error counts) and feedback-derived signals (trait-specific praise and criticism via aspect-based sentiment analysis with a DeBERTa-v3 ABSA model, confidence above 0.9) are then extracted and related to the scores. The framework was applied to GPT-3.5, GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, and Llama 2, 3, and 4 models on the ASAP and DREsS datasets to compare LLM scores with human ratings and examine how feedback sentiment and essay characteristics relate to assigned scores.
requirements: Requires datasets containing an essay prompt, a student essay response, a scoring rubric, and a human-assigned reference score
constraints: Feedback sentiment extraction retains only ABSA predictions with confidence above 0.9 and discards neutral predictions
target_learning_goals: written feedback quality and coherence with scores
examples: Applied to ASAP Task 1 (1,783 essays), ASAP Task 7 (1,569 essays), and DREsS_New (1,917 essays after filtering empty texts)

citation: Ben Swift. (2026). LLMs Unplugged: Teaching Resources for a ChatGPT World. 28th Australasian Computing Education Conference (ACE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3786228.3786237
title: LLMs Unplugged open resource suite: lessons, instructor notes, and n-gram booklet software tools at www.llmsunplugged.org
description: LLMs Unplugged is a freely available (CC BY-NC-SA) collection of unplugged activities for teaching language-model fundamentals, hosted at www.llmsunplugged.org. Its core mechanic has students build n-gram models by hand from children's books, tallying which words follow which, then generate text via weighted dice rolls. The site has three components: lessons with printable handouts, instructor notes that “explain the connection between the activity and modern LLMs,” and an optional MIT-licensed Rust/Typst software tool that tokenises any input text and produces formatted n-gram booklets for domain-relevant pre-training.
requirements: Activities work without the software tools when hand-trained on short texts; the tool is optional for scaling to longer texts and larger vocabularies
constraints: Licensed CC BY-NC-SA; the software tool is optional and activities work when hand-trained on short texts
target_learners: public servants and executives in executive education
target_learning_goals: understanding how language models are trained and generate text
examples: Example lesson handouts for Training, Generation and Pre-trained model generation are included in the paper's appendix; educators can generate custom booklets from medical case studies, legal documents, poetry, or student essays

article_title: You've Got AI Friend in Me: LLMs as Collaborative Learning Partners
citation: Daniel M. Oppenheimer, Trent N. Cash, Allison E. Connell Pensky. (2025). You've Got AI Friend in Me: LLMs as Collaborative Learning Partners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00521-6
title: LLMs as collaborative learning partners: elaboration and argumentation mechanisms applied to student-LLM interaction
description: The article extends collaborative learning theory to human-LLM collaboration. It defines collaborative learning via three components: "The learner must be working with an external entity", a shared goal, and an educational outcome. It identifies elaboration (students sharing knowledge, reinforced by LLMs' conversational prompts and responses) and argumentation (LLMs critiquing and challenging student beliefs) as the mechanisms LLMs can support, while avoiding human-team problems like social loafing. It positions LLMs as peers or sounding boards rather than expert tutors.
requirements: Students must maintain skepticism toward LLM output and engage in bi-directional elaboration and argumentation rather than offloading work or treating the LLM as an authoritative expert
constraints: Human-human collaboration is typically reciprocal whereas human-LLM interaction is not inherently beneficial to the LLM; LLMs may hallucinate or be unwilling to contradict student misunderstandings
examples: The course assignments operationalized the framework: students elaborated via 300-word argumentative essays, then prompted an LLM to critique the argument as thoroughly as possible, then rebutted or updated their argument

description: The review organizes its synthesis around four research questions: how LLMs can "foster critical thinking, collaborative skills, and problem-solving", reduce the gap between theoretical curricula and real-world skills, deliver personalized feedback in large courses, and support assessment development. It frames LLM effects as "transversal, influencing multiple dimensions of higher education systems", positioning the technology as addressing persistent problems: memorization-focused teaching, misaligned curricula, delayed feedback and limited skill development in large classes. description: The paper argues that using LLMs in education demands that teachers and learners develop competencies and literacies to understand both the technology and its limits. It states that LLMs in education "require teachers and learners to develop sets of competencies and literacies necessary to both understand the technology as well as their limitations and unexpected brittleness of such systems." citation: Steinert, S., Avila, K. E., Ruzika, S., Kuhn, J., & Küchemann, S. (2024). Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00354-1

description: The article enumerates six types of scaffolds that systematic prompting can elicit from an LLM, rooted in educational research: cognitive sense-making, cognitive elaboration, cognitive self-explanation, cognitive partial task solution, metacognitive scaffolds, and motivational scaffolds. The authors state that "these types of prompts can be combined to create a more tailored and effective feedback for the students." title: LlamaLo: an LLM chatbot fine-tuned with LoRA on ChangeMyView discussions where a Delta was awarded

examples: Developed via LoRA fine-tuning of Llama-2-7b-chat-hf on 1378 Delta-awarded CMV discussions sampled from a dataset used in prior research, then tested in ten discussions on controversial topics.

citation: Da-Wei Zhang, Melissa Boey, Yan Yu Tan & Alexis Hoh Sheng Jia. (2024). Evaluating large language models for criterion-based grading from agreement to consistency. npj Science of Learning 9:79. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00291-1

article_title: A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis
citation: Michael J. Parker, Caitlin Anderson, Claire Stone, YeaRim Oh. (2024). A Large Language Model Approach to Educational Survey Feedback Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00414-0
title: Educational survey analysis goals achieved by chaining composable LLM-performed NLP tasks into workflows
description: A framework treating educational survey analysis goals as sequences of natural language processing tasks — multi-label, multi-class, and binary classification, extraction, inductive thematic analysis, and sentiment analysis — each performed by an LLM in zero-shot mode. High-level analysis proceeds bottom-up via inductive thematic analysis or top-down via multi-label classification with predefined labels; focused analysis chains extraction followed by classification or thematic analysis, with sentiment analysis as a final step. The authors demonstrate these "composable building blocks" on real end-of-course survey comments, with quantification supported by classification counts.
requirements: Workflows require clear specification of the analysis goal in prompts, label definitions as context, and batching of comments to fit the model's context window when deriving themes.
constraints: Demonstrated on end-of-course feedback from online biomedical science courses; inductive thematic analysis lacks an accepted evaluation method, per the article.
target_learners: higher education and online course providers analyzing student feedback
target_learning_goals: deriving insights from qualitative survey feedback to improve courses and teaching
examples: Example workflows included deriving themes from Q1 comments, finding suggestions for improvement via extraction plus multi-class classification, and identifying content gaps in immunology courses.

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: LLM-embedding autograding pipeline for freeform mathematical proofs
description: The paper describes an automated grading process in which a student-written proof is first run through a pretrained large language model to obtain embeddings, and a custom classification model is then applied to those embeddings to calculate accuracy on various rubric points. constraints: Model accuracy is not guaranteed and misgrading cases were observed in user feedback; classifier is trained per rubric point and per problem, so generalization to new problems is not established
target_learners: Undergraduate students in discrete mathematics or proof-based courses

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06399-7
title: Combine AI-simulated patient conversations with structured AI-generated feedback as a cost-effective supplement to existing CDM training
description: The article recommends pairing LLM-simulated patient conversations with structured, criterion-based AI feedback when training clinical decision making. The authors conclude that "AI-simulated medical history conversations can support CDM training, especially when combined with structured feedback", positioning the format as "a cost-effective supplement to existing training methods" that offers potentially unlimited practice opportunities in number, time, and variety of cases.
requirements: The AI-generated feedback must focus solely on CDM processes rather than on transmitting medical content
Feedback should be delivered after each simulated conversation, with equal training opportunities across learners
constraints: The authors emphasize this is intended as a supplementary training resource for medical students and not as a replacement for real-life interactions
LLM simulation neglects non-verbal and social aspects of patient encounters, such as facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice
examples: In the trial, the feedback group received ChatGPT feedback during the breaks between four simulated patient cases while the control group simply paused.
